TeleTune: Evolving Agent Skills
From Offline Telemetry

Justin Chih-Yao Chen Affiliation: UNC Chapel Hill    Elias Stengel-Eskin Affiliation: Microsoft    Yan Chen Affiliation: Microsoft    Pol Llado Affiliation: Microsoft    Scott Counts Affiliation: Microsoft    Mohit Bansal Affiliation: UNC Chapel Hill   
Benjamin Van Durme Affiliation: Microsoft    Harsh Jhamtani Affiliation: Microsoft    Gaurav Verma Affiliation: Microsoft
Abstract

Computer-use agents need to capture procedural knowledge of how people use software. User telemetry, i.e., logs of interface states and user actions, offers a scalable source of this knowledge. However, learning reusable skills from these logs requires addressing three challenges: (1) Goal Underspecification, since logs do not record the goal behind each action; (2) Non-Replayability, since past activity cannot be replayed to evaluate skill updates; and (3) Interleaved Trajectories, since logs may mix several tasks without marking their boundaries. To address these challenges, we introduce TeleTune, a framework for learning a textual skill library from offline logs without recorded goals, cannot be replayed during optimization, and may interleave tasks. The library contains workflows describing cross-instance procedures and skills guiding individual task decisions, both provided as context to the agent at test time. TeleTune uses action-prediction errors on logged trajectories to propose library edits and keep only those that improve held-out action-prediction accuracy, which we call skill-guided progress. The learned workflows also enable retrieval of demonstrations that cover the subgoals of a new task. At test time, the agent is provided with the learned library and the workflow-based retrieved demonstrations. Experiments on WorkArena and Online-Mind2Web show that TeleTune outperforms random retrieval, Agent Workflow Memory (AWM), and their combination. We find that the best baseline varies by setting, whereas TeleTune achieves average success rates of 77.1%77.1\% and 80.6%80.6\%, respectively, improving over the strongest baseline on each benchmark by 6.7%6.7\% and 7.7%7.7\%. Under the heaviest perturbation of the WorkArena training data, TeleTune keeps the highest average success rate at 68.5%68.5\%, 6.3%6.3\% above the strongest baseline. Finally, our analyses show that skill optimization and workflow-based retrieval are complementary, that optimizing on fixed logs costs 5 to 75 times fewer tokens than validating the same edits with live episodes, and that skill-guided progress tracks the live success rate.

1 Introduction

Completing a task in an unfamiliar software system requires knowing more than which buttons to click. For example, an agent handling a service request may need to locate the relevant record, check its fields, and follow a local procedure before changing its status. Learning reusable skills from experience offers a way to provide agents with such procedural knowledge (Wang et al., 2025; Ouyang et al., 2026b; Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025). For agents adapting to an organization’s tools and practices, one source of this experience is user telemetry, the logs of interface states and actions recorded as people use software. These logs capture how users carry out recurring procedures and could help an agent complete similar tasks in the future. However, these logs record ongoing user activity whose goals and task boundaries are implicit, unlike the individual, goal-labeled trajectories used in the skill-learning literature. Learning from this ongoing activity raises three related challenges visualized in Figure 1(a) and (b): (1) Goal Underspecification: Logs record what a user did, but typically do not record the goal behind each action sequence. The agent must learn from actions whose purpose is implicit in the interface state and preceding history. (2) Non-Replayability: Telemetry records actions taken by real users while completing their own tasks. We cannot expect users to repeat those tasks each time we update a skill library just to help validate it. Nor do logs necessarily preserve a resettable environment in which an agent can try the task with the updated library. We must therefore evaluate skill updates offline from the recorded activity, without the fresh outcome feedback available through live interaction. (3) Interleaved Trajectories: Logs may interleave several tasks without marking their boundaries. A user might interrupt a record update to look up information elsewhere, handle an unrelated request, and then return to the original record.

Prior work addresses parts of this setting. AWM and ReasoningBank learn reusable guidance from goal-labeled experience (Wang et al., 2025; Ouyang et al., 2026b), while NNetNav and robotic process mining address goal-free exploration and unsegmented logs, respectively (Murty et al., 2024; Leno et al., 2020; Leno et al., 2021). None of these approaches addresses all three challenges together, which motivates our question: can an agent learn reusable skills from logs that carry no goals, cannot be replayed to evaluate updates, and interleave several tasks? We illustrate this setting in Figure 1 (c),

and introduce Telemetry-Informed Tuning for Agent Skills (TeleTune), a framework for learning a reusable textual skill library from offline logs without recorded goals or environment access during optimization. Our central idea is to use the prediction of recorded actions as the learning signal for building and revising the skill library. The library contains (1) workflows, describing procedures shared across task instances, and (2) skills, which guides individual decisions. Both are editable text provided in the prompt of an agent at test time. Like SkillOpt (Yang et al., 2026), we treat the skill text itself as the object of optimization and keep only edits that improve held-out performance. However, SkillOpt learns from individual tasks with known goals and validates each edit by executing tasks in a live environment. Telemetry offers none of these conditions, since its trajectories do not specify goals, cannot be replayed, and may interleave several tasks.

Concretely, TeleTune predicts the next action at each step of a logged trajectory, conditioned on the inferred goal, current library, interface state, and preceding action history. After each prediction, we append the recorded action to the history, so an early error does not derail later steps and every scoreable step contributes to the learning signal. We call the resulting action-prediction accuracy skill-guided progress. An optimizer examines the first prediction error in each trajectory and proposes additions, revisions, or removals to the entries in the library. The edits form one candidate library, which we keep only if it improves skill-guided progress on held-out trajectories. This loop allows us to refine skills using fixed logs without requesting new outcomes from the environment. Skill-guided progress can also serve as an offline proxy for the live success rate: in our WorkArena L1 run, we find that improvements in this metric track improvements in the live success rate (Figure 3). This lets us compare skill libraries using existing trajectories without a live test environment, which is often unavailable for real-world systems. At test time, TeleTune uses the learned workflows to retrieve demonstrations that together cover a new task’s subgoals. The agent then receives the task goal, the library, and these demonstrations in its prompt and acts in the live environment.

We evaluate TeleTune on WorkArena (Drouin et al., 2024; Boisvert et al., 2024) and Online-Mind2Web (Deng et al., 2023; Xue et al., 2025). WorkArena tests transfer from successful oracle trajectories to new tasks at the atomic L1 and compositional L2 levels. To isolate the effect of task interleaving, we also construct perturbed training pools with varying interruption rates. To test with human-recorded activity, we learn from annotator-recorded Mind2Web trajectories on real websites (Deng et al., 2023) and evaluate on new tasks through live website interaction (Xue et al., 2025). With GPT-5.4 as the agent, TeleTune outperforms random demonstration retrieval, Agent Workflow Memory, and their combination on both benchmarks. TeleTune reaches 92.3%92.3\% success on WorkArena L1 and 61.8%61.8\% on L2, improving over the strongest baseline by 12.0%12.0\% and 1.4%1.4\%, respectively. On Online-Mind2Web, it also reaches 80.6%80.6\% with a 7.7%7.7\% improvement. Moreover, TeleTune shows the highest average WorkArena success rate under the heaviest controlled perturbation, reaching 68.5%68.5\%, 6.3%6.3\% above the strongest baseline. Our analyses further show that (1) skill optimization and workflow-based retrieval are complementary, (2) optimizing on fixed logs costs 5 to 75 times fewer tokens than validating the same edits with live episodes, and (3) skill-guided progress tracks the live success rate during optimization. On WorkArena L1, the live success rate rises from 74.1%74.1\% to 92.3%92.3\% as skill-guided progress improves, which suggests that skill-guided progress can serve as an offline proxy for evaluating skill updates.

2 TeleTune: Telemetry-Informed Tuning for Agent Skills

2.1 Problem Formulation

We model a computer-use task as a partially observable Markov decision process, with a reward defined for a task goal gg. The agent never observes the state directly. At step tt it sees an observation oto_{t}, the current browser page in our experiments, and keeps an action history ht=(a1,…,at−1)h_{t}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{t-1}). It acts with a frozen language-model policy πθ\pi_{\theta}. The object we learn is the skill library ℳ\mathcal{M}, a text document of workflows and skills (Section 2.2) placed in the agent’s prompt and shared across tasks. During skill optimization, no recorded goal is available, and no demonstrations are retrieved. We call the policy the predictor in this phase, and we give it an inferred goal g^\hat{g} written from the recorded actions (see Section A.1 for the prompt), so the train-time policy is πθ(⋅∣g^,ot,ht,ℳ)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\hat{g},o_{t},h_{t},\mathcal{M}). At test time, we condition the agent on the task goal gg and on a set of retrieved demonstrations ℰ\mathcal{E} (Section 2.3), and it predicts the next action:

at∼πθ(⋅∣g,ot,ht,ℳ,ℰ).a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}\left(\cdot\mid g,o_{t},h_{t},\mathcal{M},\mathcal{E}\right). (1)

Our goal is to improve the agent by learning ℳ\mathcal{M} and constructing ℰ\mathcal{E} while leaving θ\theta unchanged.

Training Trajectories. We assume a collection 𝒟\mathcal{D} of successful trajectories recorded before optimization. Each trajectory τ=((o1,a1),…,(o|τ|,a|τ|))\tau=((o_{1},a_{1}),\ldots,(o_{|\tau|},a_{|\tau|})) is a sequence of interface states and the actions taken in them. We assume that each trajectory holds only states and actions, with no task goal, and that the logs cannot be replayed, so TeleTune never interacts with the training environment. We split 𝒟\mathcal{D} into a train split and a dev split. We use the train split to find the prediction errors that motivate edits and the dev split to decide whether to accept them.

Offline Evaluation by Teacher Forcing. We run the predictor step by step through each trajectory with the library in its prompt (Figure 2a). At step tt, it sees the inferred goal, the history, and on Mind2Web the recorded page oto_{t}, and predicts the next action a^t\hat{a}_{t}. We append a^t\hat{a}_{t} to the history if it matches the recorded action ata_{t} and append ata_{t} otherwise (i.e., teacher forcing). An early error therefore does not derail the rest of the trajectory, and every later step still gives feedback. We score only the actions that are predictable from the recorded context. Actions whose target is not a visible label, such as a CSS selector or a positional index like nth=0, are kept in the history but are not scored, and a prediction counts as correct when its action type matches and its target and value match closely (Appendix C). We call the per-trajectory action-prediction accuracy skill-guided progress,

Q(τ,ℳ)=1|Sτ|∑t∈Sτ𝟏[a^t=at],Q(\tau,\mathcal{M})=\frac{1}{|S_{\tau}|}\sum_{t\in S_{\tau}}\mathbf{1}\left[\hat{a}_{t}=a_{t}\right], (2)

where SτS_{\tau} is the set of scoreable steps in τ\tau.

2.2 Skill Optimization

The skill library ℳ\mathcal{M} is one structured text document that is inserted directly into the agent’s context. It contains two kinds of entries. A workflow gives the ordered steps of a procedure that recurs across tasks, with the values that vary across instances written as placeholders. A skill resolves a single decision that a procedure leaves open, such as which field to fill first or whether to enter a value exactly as the task gives it. Appendix F shows three full libraries containing both. The library starts with workflows only, induced from the training trajectories with a workflow-induction prompt (Section A.2), and with no skills. Skill optimization then repeatedly applies an offline reflect-edit-validate loop (Figure 2a). At each optimization step, we collect prediction errors on the train split, ask the optimizer to propose a small set of edits, and keep the edits only if they raise skill-guided progress QQ on the dev split. Optimization runs in two stages. The workflow stage edits only workflows, and the skill stage then edits only skills while the workflows stay fixed. Each stage ends after five consecutive steps without an accepted edit or after 25 steps (Appendix C). The predictor and the optimizer are LLMs with the same backbone as the agent used at inference time.

Reflect. Given the current library, we run the predictor through the train-split trajectories as in Section 2.1. For each trajectory with at least one error, we record the first prediction error as a failure case, consisting of the inferred goal, the preceding history, the page on Mind2Web, the predicted action, and the recorded action. The optimizer reads a fixed-size batch of these cases during the Edit step. Each case contains only what the predictor could see. The inferred goal is written from the whole trajectory and can reflect later steps, but its prompt forbids describing the action sequence (Section A.1), which limits how much the optimizer can learn about future actions from it.

Edit. The optimizer reads the failure batch, the current library ℳ\mathcal{M}, and the list of edits rejected since the last accepted step, and proposes a small set of edits that are applied together to give a candidate library ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime}. For workflows, an edit requests that a workflow be distilled, replaced, or removed. For skills, an edit adds, replaces, or removes one entry, and each new skill is a short rule tied to an observed failure. Skills are written from a single failure case, while workflows are distilled from several trajectories. Restricting the optimizer to explicit edit operations keeps each change readable and prevents it from rewriting the whole library. For example, GPT-5.4 accepted the following skill on WorkArena L1: “In list filters, if the needed value is absent or no value widget is available after setting field and operator, finish the filter by running it instead of guessing a value.” The optimizer wrote it from a single trajectory in which the recorded user left the assigned to condition empty and clicked Run, while the predictor filled in a user name. Appendix F shows full libraries.

Validate. Once per step, after the proposal, we score the candidate and current libraries on the same dev-split trajectories with skill-guided progress QQ (Section 2.1). The candidate library ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} replaces ℳ\mathcal{M} only if its mean QQ over the dev split is higher; otherwise we keep ℳ\mathcal{M}. We checkpoint accepted libraries and record rejected edits. We include the rejected edits in the optimizer’s input in later steps, so it does not propose the same change again. In summary, reflection proposes changes from observed failures, validation keeps only those that transfer to the dev split, and the overall pipeline does not require an online environment.

2.3 Workflow-Based Retrieval

Workflow-based retrieval gives the agent demonstrations that cover the subgoals a new task requires. Learned abstractions are often not enough on their own, since the agent also needs to see the contexts in which they are used (Zheng et al., 2024; Stengel-Eskin et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). Similarity-based retrieval is one option, but on compositional tasks it often returns several demonstrations of the same operation. In our preliminary experiment, with k=8k{=}8, it performs similarly to Random-kk on WorkArena L1 (+2.1%+2.1\%) but falls below it on L2 (−4.5%-4.5\%). We instead use the optimized workflows 𝒲∗\mathcal{W}^{*} as an intermediate representation between task goals and trajectories. Offline, each training trajectory is annotated with the workflows it instantiates, and common workflows are down-weighted so that generic operations do not dominate. For a new task, a planner decomposes the task goal into subgoals and maps each subgoal to candidate workflows. A training trajectory covers a subgoal when the workflows it instantiates include one the planner matched to that subgoal, and the match clears a confidence threshold. A greedy selector then repeatedly picks the trajectory that covers the most still-uncovered subgoals, until every subgoal is covered, no confident match remains, or the demonstration budget is reached. The greedy selector thus favors complementary demonstrations over redundant neighbors. Appendix B gives the weighting, the relevance score, and the selection rule; Table 3 compares this selector with random retrieval.

2.4 Inference

After optimization, the final skill library ℳ∗\mathcal{M}^{*} is fixed and shared across all test tasks. For each task goal gg, retrieval builds ℰ\mathcal{E} once before interaction begins, and the prompt then holds the task goal, the library, and the retrieved demonstrations (Figure 2b). The task goal gg is available to both the retrieval planner and the agent, while the retrieved demonstrations carry no goals of their own. At each step, the agent predicts an action with Equation 1, executes it, observes the resulting page, and extends its history, while the library and demonstrations stay fixed. TeleTune therefore adapts at two levels. Skill optimization learns global knowledge that transfers across tasks, and workflow-based retrieval assembles local evidence to cover subgoals of the current task.

3 Experimental Setup

Dataset. We evaluate TeleTune on two datasets. (1) WorkArena: a suite of knowledge-work tasks on a live ServiceNow instance (Drouin et al., 2024). L1 tasks are generally easier and consist of atomic operations such as filling a form. L2 tasks are from WorkArena++ (Boisvert et al., 2024), compose several such operations under one instruction and require the agent to carry information between them. We prune task families whose oracle is unsuitable for learning or evaluation: those with empty action traces, whose expert policy fails because of broken ServiceNow fixtures or controls, and L2 tasks whose solution is to report infeasibility. This leaves 270 training and 270 test instances on L1, and 216 training and 198 test instances on L2. (2) Mind2Web: we train on annotator-recorded trajectories from the original Mind2Web training set (Deng et al., 2023) and evaluate through live interaction on Online-Mind2Web (Xue et al., 2025). To align the training and test domains and to reduce cost, we keep only test tasks whose website category also appears in the original Mind2Web training set, and we downsample the training trajectories to follow the test category distribution (details in Appendix D). This yields 640 training trajectories and 122 test tasks. Table 6 provides more detailed statistics on both datasets. We would like to highlight that Online-Mind2Web matches our setting directly. The training data are trajectories recorded on real websites in the past, and evaluation asks the agent to complete new tasks on live sites, with no guarantee that the recorded trajectories can be replayed since the sites may have changed. All training data are goal-free, i.e., only at test time, the agent will receive a task goal.

Models. We use GPT-5.4 for the main results and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 and Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B for the cross-model analysis.11 1 Hereafter, we refer to them as GPT-5.4, Qwen-3.6, and Mistral-3.5, respectively. Each backbone learns its own skill library. The same backbone infers the goals, induces the workflows, optimizes the skills, and acts as the agent at test time, so an agent is always paired with the library learned by its own backbone.

Baselines. Naive runs the agent with the task goal and uses no training trajectories. Random-kk adds k=8k=8 randomly sampled training demonstrations, which carry no goals. AWM (Wang et al., 2025) induces workflows from recurring subroutines in the training trajectories and places them in the prompt. AWM ++ Random-kk combines the two. In our workflow-based retrieval, we also use k=8k=8 training demonstrations. All methods share the same model, test tasks, and step budget. As with TeleTune, AWM induces its workflows with the agent’s own backbone.

Evaluation Protocol. Every method runs on the same test tasks with three seeds. On WorkArena, the maximum step budget is set to 100 steps for L1 and 200 for L2. On Online-Mind2Web, the step budget is set to 200. Following Xue et al. (2025), we judge the completed trajectories with WebJudge using o4-mini. WebJudge extracts the instruction’s requirements, selects relevant screenshots, and returns a binary verdict for the task. Live websites sometimes block automated browsers with a CAPTCHA or a bot-detection page, which stops the agent from completing the task. On Online-Mind2Web, we therefore report a discounted success rate, which excludes episodes that hit such a page and computes success over the remaining episodes.

4 Results and Analysis

4.1 Main Results

TeleTune outperforms all baselines on both benchmarks. We first compare TeleTune with the baselines using GPT-5.4 as the agent (Table 1). TeleTune achieves the best success rate across different levels and benchmarks. On WorkArena, it reaches 77.1%77.1\% on average, 6.7%6.7\% above the strongest baseline (AWM ++ Random-kk), and shows the largest gain on L1 (80.3%→92.3%80.3\%\rightarrow 92.3\%). On Online-Mind2Web, it reaches 80.6%80.6\%, 7.7%7.7\% above Random-kk, and the largest gain is on hard tasks (64.7%→75.3%64.7\%\rightarrow 75.3\%). Combining the two baselines does not always help. AWM ++ Random-kk is the strongest baseline on WorkArena, yet on Online-Mind2Web it falls below both AWM and Random-kk (70.2%70.2\% versus 71.9%71.9\% and 72.9%72.9\%). On WorkArena L2, TeleTune leads AWM ++ Random-kk by 1.4%1.4\%, a smaller margin than on L1. We propose two reasons for this. First, fewer optimization steps were accepted on L2 than on L1 (4 versus 14, Table 4). L2 has 216 training trajectories spread over 72 task templates, about 33 per template against 3030 on L1 (Table 6), so an edit written from one failure has few similar dev trajectories on which to raise skill-guided progress. The same sparsity may explain why similarity-based retrieval falls below Random-kk on L2 but not on L1 (Section 2.3). With few demonstrations per template, the nearest neighbors of an L2 task tend to repeat one operation, while random samples cover more task families. Second, L2 require about three times as many steps as L1 tasks (Table 9) and require carrying information between operations. Thus, adding skills for individual decisions may not address the primary bottlenecks for L2 tasks.

TeleTune generalizes to other backbones. Next, we test whether TeleTune also helps agents built on other backbones (Table 2). For each backbone, we rerun the full pipeline, so Qwen-3.6 and Mistral-3.5 each learn their own library from the same training trajectories and use it at test time. With Qwen-3.6 as the agent, TeleTune is again the best method on both WorkArena levels. It reaches 75.6%75.6\% on L1 and 50.0%50.0\% on L2, which is 11.9%11.9\% and 5.1%5.1\% above AWM ++ Random-kk. With Mistral-3.5, TeleTune is on par with the strongest baseline. It leads AWM by 0.5%0.5\% on L1 and falls behind Random-kk by 1.1%1.1\% on L2. Overall, TeleTune generalizes to other backbones when each backbone learns its own library.

4.2 Ablations and Analysis

Skill-guided progress is an offline proxy for the live success rate. Like prior work, we evaluate every method in live environments. However, many real-world software systems offer no live environment even for evaluation, and logs cannot be replayed. We therefore test whether skill-guided progress on the dev split can stand in for the live success rate, which would make it useful for comparing skill libraries even outside our optimization loop. Figure 3 traces the optimization run on WorkArena L1, where we also evaluate four of the accepted libraries live. In the workflow stage (steps 1 to 9), skill-guided progress on the dev split stays near 50%50\%. The skill stage starting at step 10 raises skill-guided progress to 73.0%73.0\%, with the largest increase at its first step. Over the same run, the live success rate rises from 74.1%74.1\% to 83.1%83.1\%, 88.7%88.7\%, and 92.3%92.3\%, in the same order as skill-guided progress. Since the live success rate is never used during optimization, this suggests that skill-guided progress can serve as an offline proxy for it.

Skill optimization and workflow-based retrieval are complementary. In Table 3, we toggle the two components of TeleTune, skill optimization and workflow-based retrieval. Skill optimization is the larger single factor. With random retrieval, it improves success by 18.6%18.6\% on L1, 6.6%6.6\% on L2, and 2.2%2.2\% on Online-Mind2Web. Workflow-based retrieval does little without the library (+1.7%+1.7\% on L1, −1.6%-1.6\% on L2, and +1.4%+1.4\% on OM2W), which suggests that matched demonstrations transfer poorly on their own. With the learned library, however, workflow-based retrieval adds 8.6%8.6\%, 1.0%1.0\%, and 5.5%5.5\%, respectively, so the two components are complementary. On L1, the full TeleTune is 27.2%27.2\% above the variant with neither component, which exceeds the sum of the two individual gains by 6.9%6.9\%. This also extends to L2 (+2.6%+2.6\%) and OM2W (+4.1%+4.1\%).

TeleTune keeps the highest average success on noisy training pools. To test learning from interleaved tasks under controlled conditions, we perturb the WorkArena training pool with an interruption rate qq and rebuild every method from the perturbed pool. Specifically, we split each training trajectory into chunks of 2 to 5 actions and, before each chunk, insert with probability qq the next chunk of a secondary task drawn from the other training tasks. The number of secondary tasks grows with qq (⌈3​q⌉\lceil 3q\rceil), and each secondary task advances in order, so a perturbed trajectory switches back and forth between coherent tasks as an interrupted user would. We use q∈{0.33,0.66,1.0}q\in\{0.33,0.66,1.0\}. Figure 4 shows success as qq grows. TeleTune has the highest success on both levels at every qq except L1 at q=1.0q{=}1.0, where it is 1.1%1.1\% below Random-kk. In contrast, AWM’s L1 success falls by 26.4%26.4\% to 49.3%49.3\%, only 3.7%3.7\% above the naive agent, which uses no training trajectories at all. We hypothesize that the gap comes from how each method uses the perturbed trajectories. Each perturbed trajectory mixes chunks from up to four tasks, so the same eight demonstrations show the agent more distinct operations than eight clean ones. AWM instead compresses the pool into abstract workflows, which can reduce this diversity. TeleTune keeps a library entry only if it improves skill-guided progress on the dev split, making it more robust to interleaved tasks.

Optimization is a one-time, offline cost. Table 4 reports the cost of learning the library. We pay this cost only once, since we learn one library per setting and reuse it unchanged across every test task and all three evaluation seeds. Almost all of the tokens are spent by the predictor scoring candidate libraries on the dev split, and the optimizer accounts for under 0.5%0.5\%. This is far less than validating the same candidates with live episodes. On L1, running each of the 32 candidates on the 138 dev tasks would take 4,416 live episodes, or about 2.8B input tokens at TeleTune’s 636.9K per episode, which is 16 times our total. The same comparison gives about 75 times on L2 and 5 times on Mind2Web. Live validation would also need a resettable environment for every dev task, which logs do not provide. We instead score fixed logs and never execute actions, so optimization does not require costly environment setup or iteration.

TeleTune trades a longer prompt for higher success. TeleTune achieves the highest success rate in every column of Table 1, and this comes with more input tokens. On L1, it uses 636.9K input tokens per episode against 343.4K to 386.1K for the baselines (Table 8). The overhead comes from a longer per-step prompt, not from longer episodes. TeleTune uses 20.3K input tokens per L1 step, compared with 11.2K to 12.9K for the other methods, while its episode length (31.4 steps) stays within the baseline range of 27.4 to 34.4 steps (Table 9). On L2, it takes the fewest steps of any method (90.0 versus 94.3 to 121.2), so it uses about as many input tokens as the naive agent (1.52M versus 1.49M). The main cause is the library, which is included in the prompt at every step. The final L1 library has 56 skills and 6.4K tokens, and re-sending it on each of about 31 steps accounts for roughly 201K tokens per episode. We also tried giving the Random-kk baseline more input tokens to see whether that closes the gap. With k=30k{=}30, Random-kk uses 504.2K input tokens per L1 episode but reaches only 63.7%63.7\%, below its 65.1%65.1\% with k=8k{=}8. We also note that while output tokens are usually more expensive than input, the output length is almost unaffected (3.1K tokens per L1 episode, within the 2.3K to 3.4K range of the baselines). Since the library is a fixed part of the prompt, prompt caching can reuse it across steps, and a per-task skill retriever, analogous to workflow-based retrieval, could reduce the per-step cost further. We leave this to future work.

5 Related Work

Learning Agent Skills From Experience. A growing body of work improves LLM agents with reusable knowledge learned from experience, including executable skills and abstractions (Wang et al., 2023; Stengel-Eskin et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025), natural-language insights and trajectory-derived guidance (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Ouyang et al., 2026b; Ni et al., 2026), retrieved past trajectories (Zheng et al., 2024), and hindsight rewrites of failed trajectories (Hu et al., 2026). Other work uses reinforcement learning to improve skill use and generation (Wu et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Ouyang et al., 2026a), or refines prompts, skills, and other artifacts with execution feedback (Agrawal et al., 2026; Alzubi et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Qiu et al., 2026). Like these methods, our optimization is a gradient-free, discrete search over edits, but it edits a structured library and scores candidates by teacher-forced action prediction on fixed logs. Closest to our procedure, SkillOpt (Yang et al., 2026) keeps bounded edits to a skill document that improve held-out task performance, but it validates each candidate by executing tasks. TeleTune instead uses skill-guided progress, which needs no live environment or new execution outcomes.

Learning From Demonstrations and Activity Logs. Learning procedural knowledge from recorded behavior connects to imitation learning (Ross et al., 2011), goal-conditioned learning (Andrychowicz et al., 2017), and temporal abstraction through options (Klissarov and Precup, 2021). Closer to our setting, AWM (Wang et al., 2025) induces textual workflows from goal-labeled trajectories, and NNetNav (Murty et al., 2024) explores websites without predefined goals, labels the resulting trajectories with instructions, and fine-tunes a browser agent. Robotic process mining discovers recurring routines in user-interface logs, including unsegmented logs with unrelated events (Leno et al., 2021; Leno et al., 2020). SkillClaw (Ma et al., 2026) learns a shared skill repository from multi-user agent interactions, but its logs include task goals, and its validation reruns tasks in users’ environments. Our work differs from these approaches in two ways. First, we learn a textual skill library from logs without recorded task goals. Second, we evaluate updates against recorded actions without task replay, even when the logs interleave several tasks.

6 Conclusion

We introduced TeleTune, a framework that learns a textual skill library from offline logs that record no goals, cannot be replayed, and may interleave tasks. Using the recorded actions as supervision, TeleTune infers a goal for each trajectory, proposes library edits from action-prediction errors, and keeps an edit only when it raises skill-guided progress on held-out trajectories. At test time, the learned workflows retrieve demonstrations that cover a new task’s subgoals. TeleTune outperforms retrieval and workflow-induction baselines on WorkArena and Online-Mind2Web, raising average success over the strongest baseline by 6.7%6.7\% and 7.7%7.7\%. It also leads with Qwen-3.6 and matches the strongest baseline with Mistral-3.5. On WorkArena L1, the live success rate rises with skill-guided progress during optimization (74.1%→92.3%74.1\%\rightarrow 92.3\%). TeleTune keeps the highest average success under the heaviest task interleaving. Skill optimization and workflow-based retrieval are complementary, and scoring edits on fixed logs costs 5 to 75 times fewer tokens than live validation. Overall, these results suggest that the logs people already leave while using software can teach an agent reusable skills and show whether a skill update helps without a live environment.

Appendix

Appendix A Prompts

The goal-inference prompt (Section A.1) gives each training trajectory the inferred goal g^\hat{g} that the predictor conditions on (Section 2.1), and the workflow-induction prompt (Section A.2) builds the initial workflows of the library (Section 2.2). During optimization, the optimizer proposes edits with the prompt in Section A.3, and the predictor predicts actions with the prompt in Section A.4. At test time, the agent receives the help text in Section A.5, and workflow-based retrieval uses the prompts in Section A.6. Placeholders in angle brackets, such as <SKILL_LIBRARY>, stand for content filled in at run time.

A.1 Goal-Inference Prompt

Recall that the training trajectories carry no goals, so during skill optimization the predictor receives an inferred goal g^\hat{g} (Section 2.1). Before optimization, we infer one goal per train and dev trajectory with the backbone at temperature 0. WorkArena and Mind2Web use the two system prompts below, and both share the user message that follows. If an output breaks a rule, for example by exceeding the word limit or listing UI actions, we append the reason to the user message and ask again, up to five attempts. The inferred goals are cached and reused across optimization steps.

⬇ You reconstruct the most specific plausible user request behind one successful ServiceNow/WorkArena UI trajectory instance. Produce a concise desired-outcome sentence, not instructions for carrying it out. Grounding and anti-leakage rules: - Output exactly <intent>ONE sentence of at most 50 words</intent> and nothing else. The tags are formatting and are removed before the intent is stored. - Preserve every task-defining detail recoverable from the trajectory: the target record or object type (incident, problem, change request, hardware asset, user, expense line, catalog item, ...), the operation performed, and the concrete values that shaped it -- short descriptions, categories, impact, urgency, priority, filter criteria, amounts, dates, or quantities. Exact task values are useful and should not be replaced by vague words such as "specified", "chosen", or "desired". - Infer only details supported by the actions; a filled field or selected option expresses a user constraint, not merely a UI instruction. - Do not list, paraphrase, or imply an ordered sequence of UI actions. - Do not use action verbs as UI commands (click, fill, select, press, navigate). - Do not mention selectors, element IDs, application or module names, generic control labels, or the mechanics of operating the page. - Do not expose passwords, personal contact details, authentication data, or opaque record numbers; describe those only as the required account or contact information. - If a detail is uncertain, omit only that detail; do not generalize away other constraints the trace clearly supports. Good: <intent>Create a hardware incident for an overheating laptop with high impact and medium urgency.</intent> Bad (too vague): <intent>Create an incident record with the specified details.</intent> Bad (action recipe): <intent>Open Incident, fill Short description, then set Impact and Urgency.</intent>
⬇ You reconstruct the most specific plausible user goal behind one successful Mind2Web trajectory. Produce a concise desired-outcome sentence, not instructions for carrying it out. Grounding and anti-leakage rules: - Output exactly <intent>ONE sentence of at most 50 words</intent> and nothing else. The tags are formatting and are removed before the intent is stored. - Preserve every non-sensitive task-defining detail recoverable from the trajectory: named products, events, venues and destinations; dates or time ranges; quantities and variants; categories, filters, accessibility needs, sort preferences, and requested final state. Exact task values are useful and should not be replaced by vague words such as "specified", "chosen", or "desired". - Infer only details supported by the actions. A clicked event, category, filter, product, or result may express a user constraint rather than merely a UI instruction. - Do not list or imply an ordered sequence of UI actions. - Do not use action verbs as UI commands (click, fill, select, press, navigate). - Do not mention selectors, element IDs, generic control labels, or the mechanics of operating the page. - Do not expose passwords, payment-card data, personal contact details, authentication data, or opaque record identifiers. Describe those only as required contact, payment, or account information. - If a detail is uncertain, omit only that detail; do not generalize away other constraints that the trace clearly supports. Good: <intent>Find the cheapest wheelchair-accessible parking near Busch Stadium for the Pittsburgh Pirates at St. Louis Cardinals event.</intent> Bad (too vague): <intent>Find and filter accessible parking options near a specified venue.</intent> Bad (action recipe): <intent>Fill the parking search, click the event, open Filter, choose wheelchair, and sort by price.</intent>

A.2 Workflow-Induction Prompt

Recall that the library starts with workflows only, before any skill is added (Section 2.2). We initialize the workflows 𝒲\mathcal{W} with a single call to the backbone over all training trajectories. The backbone sees only the recorded action sequences, because the trajectories carry no goals. WorkArena and Mind2Web use the two prompts below. Each prompt consists of an instruction and a one-shot example, and the recorded action sequences follow in the format of the last box. The original Mind2Web one-shot example lists a goal above each action sequence, and we remove those lines so that the example matches the goal-free input.

⬇ ### Role & objective You are a workflow manager for a WorkArena agent operating in ServiceNow. You are given a batch of action sequences that completed enterprise tasks in that environment. Your job is to distill this batch into a library of reusable sub-routines ("workflows") that a future agent can compose to solve unseen tasks. ### What makes a good workflow A workflow captures a recurring intent (e.g. "create_a_record", "apply_a_filter", "sort_a_list"), not a single task instance. Extract a workflow only when the same action pattern appears, i.e., allow for parameter differences across two or more distinct tasks. For each workflow: 1. Include at least two ordered steps. 2. Replace anything that varies between instances with a typed placeholder in angle brackets: <LIST_NAME>, <FIELD>, <VALUE>, <OPERATOR>, <DIRECTION>. After drafting, verify: (1) every workflow is grounded in two or more distinct input action sequences. (2) no two workflows overlap in purpose, (3) placeholders cover only variable elements, (4) you have generate as many workflows as needed to cover all the tasks. Silently revise until all four hold. ### Output format Return only the workflow library, nothing else: Workflow: <name> Description: <when to use this workflow: the goal/intent it serves, any preconditions or entry state it assumes, and the outcome it produces> 1. <action> # comment with example value(s) 2. <action> ... Workflow: sort_list Description: Use when a ServiceNow list must be ordered by one or more fields. Preconditions: the target list is visible. Open the list builder, add one sort row per requested field, and set each row's direction. Outcome: the visible records are ordered by the configured sort levels. 1. click('.list_filter_toggle') 2. click('role=button') # add a sort row 3. select_option(<SORT_ROW>, <FIELD>) # e.g. 'nth=1', 'Assigned' 4. select_option(<SORT_ROW>, <DIRECTION>) # e.g. 'nth=1', 'ascending' 5. Repeat steps 2-4 for each additional sort level # e.g. 'City', 'descending' 6. click('Run filter')
⬇ ### Role & objective You are a workflow manager for a Mind2Web agent operating across many unrelated public websites. You are given offline Mind2Web gold action sequences expressed as click(<VISIBLE_LABEL>), fill(<VISIBLE_LABEL>, <VALUE>), and select_option(<VISIBLE_LABEL>, <OPTION>). Your job is to distill this batch into a library of reusable, website-agnostic sub-routines ("workflows") that a future agent can compose to solve unseen tasks on unfamiliar sites. ### What makes a good workflow A workflow captures a recurring cross-site intent (e.g. "complete_contact_form", "search_then_filter", "select_item_and_open_details"), not a single website or task instance. Extract a workflow only when the same semantic action pattern appears across two or more distinct tasks. Generalize site-specific visible labels when they vary; do not invent controls or selectors absent from the input. For each workflow: 1. Include at least two ordered steps. 2. Replace anything that varies between instances with a typed placeholder in angle brackets: <FIELD>, <VALUE>, <OPTION>, <ITEM>, <SUBMIT_CONTROL>. Keep a visible control label literal only when it is invariant in the supporting traces; otherwise parameterize it. Empty or noisy labels in a trace are not reusable selectors. After drafting, verify: (1) every workflow is grounded in two or more distinct input action sequences, (2) no two workflows overlap in purpose, (3) placeholders cover only variable elements, (4) you have generated as many workflows as needed to cover all the tasks. Silently revise until all four hold. ### Output format Return only the workflow library, nothing else: Workflow: <name> Description: <when to use this workflow: the goal/intent it serves, any preconditions or entry state it assumes, and the outcome it produces> 1. <action> # comment with example value(s) 2. <action> ... ## Concrete Examples Actions: click("") fill("First Name (required)", "Allan") fill("Last Name (required)", "Smith") fill("Email Address (required)", "allan.smith@gmail.com") fill("Confirm Email Address (required)", "allan.smith@gmail.com") fill("ZIP Code (required)", "10001") click("Submit") Actions: click("Demo Drive") click("Model Y") fill("Last Name", "Adams") fill("First Name", "Roy") fill("Phone Number", "123-999-0000") fill("Email Address", "RA@gmail.com") fill("Zip Code", "90001") click("Submit and Continue") ## Summary Workflows Workflow: complete_contact_form Description: Use when a public website asks for a person's contact details before a signup or request can be submitted. Preconditions: the contact form is visible. Outcome: the supplied details are submitted and the site advances to confirmation or the next step. 1. fill(<FIRST_NAME_FIELD>, <FIRST_NAME>) # e.g. "First Name (required)" 2. fill(<LAST_NAME_FIELD>, <LAST_NAME>) # e.g. "Last Name" 3. fill(<EMAIL_FIELD>, <EMAIL>) # e.g. "Email Address" 4. fill(<ADDITIONAL_CONTACT_FIELD>, <VALUE>) # repeat only for requested visible fields 5. click(<SUBMIT_CONTROL>) # e.g. "Submit", "Submit and Continue"

A.3 Optimizer Prompt

At every optimization step, the optimizer receives the system prompt below, followed by a stage-specific suffix, and the user message in the last box of this subsection. The prompt is shared across stages and still describes a trace buffer, which is disabled in all our runs, so the optimizer never sees a trace menu. The suffix restricts the allowed operations to the current stage. <MAX_EDITS> is the per-step edit limit (Table 5). On Mind2Web, the first sentence ends with “general web-navigation tasks across many unrelated public websites” instead of “ServiceNow / WorkArena tasks”, and the Mind2Web rules box is appended to the system prompt. On WorkArena, the page evidence of each case reads “(unavailable)”, because the recorded trajectories hold no page observations. A distill_workflow or replace_workflow edit is resolved by a second call with the workflow-distillation prompt at the end of this subsection.

⬇ You improve a reusable SKILL that helps a web agent predict the correct next action on ServiceNow / WorkArena tasks. The skill has THREE editable sections and you are given a batch of cases the agent got WRONG: for each, the goal, the actions already taken, the agent's PREDICTED next action, and the CORRECT next action. Editable sections: 1. SKILLS -- a numbered list of general guidance. Edit with add / replace / delete (ids refer to the skill numbers). 2. WORKFLOWS -- a library of reusable parameterised sub-routines induced from real traces. You do NOT hand-write these; instead: - distill_workflow: name a task template and a fresh workflow is induced from that task's oracle traces and appended. - replace_workflow: replace workflow #id with one freshly distilled from the named task. - delete_workflow: remove workflow #id. 3. TRACES -- a buffer of reference trajectories injected as in-context examples. Starts EMPTY and grows as you see failures: add_trace pulls in a pool menu item, delete_trace evicts a slot that is no longer useful, and replace_trace swaps one slot for a better menu item in a single move. The buffer holds at most 8 traces at a time -- once full you must delete_trace or replace_trace before adding more. Use the RIGHT lever for each error pattern: - A wrong value / which-field / verb choice that GENERALISES -> a SKILLS edit. - Every added or replaced SKILL must preserve the general rule and then include one concrete supporting example copied from the mispredicted cases, using this exact shape: "<general rule> Example: for goal '<goal>', after <relevant actions or 'no prior actions'>, the correct next action is <gold action> (not <predicted action>)." The example is evidence from a TRAINING reflection case, not a claim about the untouched test set. Quote the actual goal and actions closely enough that a reader can audit which mistake motivated the skill; concrete values are allowed in the Example clause, but the general rule before it must remain reusable. - A missing procedure for a whole task family -> distill_workflow for that task. - Workflows must be compositional and uniquely named: prefer reusable UI operations over table-specific or fixed-cardinality variants, and replace or delete an overlapping workflow instead of adding another name for it. - The in-context examples don't cover the failing task family -> add_trace (or replace_trace if the buffer is full) to bring in a relevant example (pick a menu item whose task matches the failing cases). - An existing trace is redundant or irrelevant to any recent failure -> delete_trace to make room. Hard constraints: - Do NOT hard-code instance-specific values (names, numbers, ids) in the general-rule part of a skill; those do not generalize. They may appear only in the required concrete Example clause. - Keep each skill concise, imperative, and <= 600 characters including its required Example clause. - Prefer editing/merging existing items over piling on near-duplicates. - Propose at most <MAX_EDITS> edits. Reply with STRICT JSON only, no prose, no code fences: {"edits": [ {"op": "add", "text": "<new skill>", "reason": "<why>"}, {"op": "replace", "id": <skill#>, "text": "<skill>", "reason": "<why>"}, {"op": "delete", "id": <skill#>, "reason": "<why>"}, {"op": "distill_workflow", "task": "<task_name>", "reason": "<why>"}, {"op": "replace_workflow", "id": <workflow#>, "task": "<task_name>", "reason": "<why>"}, {"op": "delete_workflow", "id": <workflow#>, "reason": "<why>"}, {"op": "add_trace", "add": <menu_id>, "reason": "<why>"}, {"op": "replace_trace", "evict": <slot#>, "add": <menu_id>, "reason": "<why>"}, {"op": "delete_trace", "evict": <slot#>, "reason": "<why>"} ]} If no edit would help, reply {"edits": []}.
⬇ Mind2Web-specific rules: - A case header has the form "Case N [task_name]". Its task_name is one of the train-derived semantic intent clusters (for example travel_search or contact_form_completion) and is the exact key required by the trace pool. - When a goal is blank, first infer internally what the task is about from the action history and CURRENT PAGE EVIDENCE. Use action verbs, visible labels, values already present in the history, and ordering to identify reusable guidance. The correct next action is a training label used to diagnose the error, not information the deployed predictor will possess. Never write a general rule that requires knowing a requested entity, value, destination, or goal that is absent from both the displayed goal and prior actions. In particular, with a blank goal and no prior actions, do not invent hidden task intent from the correct action or task_name; propose only a genuinely page-observable default, or no skill edit. - For SKILLS, ground the general rule in distinctions visible in CURRENT PAGE EVIDENCE and the action history. The semantic task_name and correct action are optimizer-only TRAIN metadata and must not become hidden prerequisites of the rule. Treat task_name as a broad family, not as a full description of the current page or instance. - For distill_workflow or replace_workflow, copy `task` EXACTLY from one of the supplied case-header task names. Do not invent a narrower family name; describe refinements in `reason` instead. This exact-copy rule lets the resolver retrieve all TRAIN oracle traces in that semantic cluster.
⬇ THIS ROUND you may use ONLY these ops: delete_workflow, distill_workflow, replace_workflow. Propose no other op type; reply {"edits": []} if none of these would help. WORKFLOW-ONLY ROUND: every supplied case is evidence that the current workflow library failed to guide the correct next action. For this round, OVERRIDE the earlier right-lever rule that assigns wrong field, value, or verb choices to SKILLS; skills are unavailable, so express a plausible procedural correction by replacing the matching workflow. Existing coverage of a case's task family is NOT by itself a reason to return no edits. If a matching workflow exists, propose replace_workflow using that workflow's id and copy the case-header task_name exactly. Use distill_workflow only when no existing workflow covers the family, and delete_workflow only for clear redundancy. You propose candidates; a downstream evaluation gate, not you, decides whether they help. With non-empty cases, do not return an empty edit list unless no legal workflow op can be formed from the displayed workflows and case task names.
⬇ THIS ROUND you may use ONLY these ops: add, delete, replace. Propose no other op type; reply {"edits": []} if none of these would help. ID SCOPE: 'id' in replace/delete refers ONLY to the SKILLS numbering (### Skills). The ### Workflows list is READ-ONLY context this round -- never use a workflow number as a skill id. Do not propose delete/replace for a skill id that is not present in the current SKILLS list. PREFER ADDING new, DISTINCT skills that cover error patterns not yet addressed. Do NOT repeatedly rewrite an existing skill that is already working -- only replace one if it is clearly wrong or superseded. Every add/replace text MUST contain an 'Example:' copied from one of the supplied training reflection cases, including that case's goal and correct next action. SKILLS-OVER-WORKFLOWS ROUND: the displayed workflows are already active READ-ONLY guidance. Add a skill only for a decision, disambiguation, or recovery rule that the workflows do not encode. Do not paraphrase a workflow's procedure into a broad skill; duplicated guidance adds prompt noise and can make action selection worse.
⬇ You are a workflow manager for a web-navigation agent. From the successful action traces of a single ServiceNow / WorkArena task template, distill ONE reusable sub-routine ("workflow") that a future agent can compose to solve unseen tasks. A workflow captures a recurring intent (e.g. "create_a_record", "apply_a_ filter", "sort_a_list"), not one task instance. Capture the COMMON action sequence shared across the given traces; drop steps that appear in only one trace. Requirements: - Give it a verb-based snake_case name describing the operation, never a table, record, seed, or count (apply_filter, not filter_incidents_by_priority). - Include at least two ordered steps in the action vocabulary (click/fill/select_option/set_checked/...). - Replace anything that varies between instances with a typed placeholder in angle brackets: <LIST_NAME>, <FIELD>, <VALUE>, <OPERATOR>, <DIRECTION>. Keep invariant labels (menu/list/button names such as "All", "New", "Submit") verbatim. - Make repeated structure compositional: say "for each condition/field/sort key" and parameterise its field, operator, connector, value, and direction. Never hard-code the number of conditions, fields, keys, or repeated steps. - Prefer the shortest correct sequence; do not invent steps not supported by the traces. Output ONLY the single workflow, nothing else (no prose, no code fences): Workflow: <name> Description: <one line: when to use this> 1. <action> # comment with example value(s) 2. <action> ...

A.4 Predictor Prompt

The predictor uses a benchmark-specific system prompt. When the library is non-empty, we append the header ## Skill (learned guidance for this task family) and then the library, i.e., the numbered skills (in the skill stage) followed by the workflows. The user message holds the inferred goal and the history. On Mind2Web, it also starts with the recorded page observation, i.e., the website, URL, pruned accessibility tree, candidate elements, cleaned DOM, and visible text. The WorkArena user message has no observation block.

⬇ You are simulating a ServiceNow / WorkArena web agent. Given the task goal and the browser actions already taken, output the SINGLE next action that makes progress toward completing the goal. Action vocabulary -- use the element's VISIBLE LABEL as the first argument (never a numeric id): click("<label>") fill("<label>", "<value>") select_option("<label>", "<value>") set_checked("<label>", "<true|false>") press("<label>", "<key>") noop(<milliseconds>) Rules: - Output ONLY the single next action call, on one line. No prose, no code fences. - Take field labels and values verbatim from the goal where applicable. - Predict exactly one action (the immediate next step), not the whole plan.
⬇ You are simulating a general web-navigation agent across many unrelated public websites. Given the task goal (when available) and the browser actions already taken, output the SINGLE next action that makes progress toward the task. Action vocabulary -- use the element's VISIBLE LABEL as the first argument (never a numeric id, CSS selector, XPath, or backend-node id): click("<label>") fill("<label>", "<value>") select_option("<label>", "<value>") set_checked("<label>", "<true|false>") press("<label>", "<key>") noop(<milliseconds>) Rules: - Output ONLY the single next action call, on one line. Do not output your inference, reasoning, prose, or code fences. - Use visible labels and task-specific values supported by the goal and history. - Do not assume controls from an enterprise app or transfer labels from an unrelated website. - Predict exactly one action (the immediate next step), not the whole plan. - Ground the action in the current Mind2Web page observation. Prefer candidate visible labels and accessible names; use the pruned tree, nearby cleaned DOM, URL/website, and visible page text to disambiguate controls. Never output a candidate id as the action target. - When the goal is blank, first infer internally what kind of task or reusable workflow is underway from the actions already taken: their verbs, visible labels, entered values, and order. Then use that inferred intent together with the learned workflows and skills to choose the next action. Revise the inferred intent as more actions arrive; do not emit the inferred intent. - When both the goal and action history are empty, no task-specific intent can be inferred. Follow only broadly applicable learned guidance; never invent a task-specific value or claim that an unseen control is present.

A.5 Agent Prompt

At test time, the WorkArena agent is the AgentLab GenericAgent, and the Online-Mind2Web agent is a Browser Use agent. We keep their own system prompts and add the help text below. On WorkArena, the help text goes into the agent’s extra instructions, after the task goal that AgentLab provides, and all kk retrieved demonstrations appear in one list without their goals. On Online-Mind2Web, the help text is placed before the task, and matched demonstrations are listed with the subgoals they cover, separately from the randomly sampled ones.

⬇ You are about to solve a Web Agentic task. You are given two kinds of optional reference material below. (1) Skills and Workflows. These are HIGHER LEVEL: it describes reusable procedures, behavioral guidance, and overall step patterns, and may omit low-level interaction details. (2) The REFERENCE TRAJECTORIES are LOWER LEVEL: they contain concrete action sequences from previously attempted tasks. Take the trajectories only as references for how individual UI interactions can be carried out when applicable. They are not necessarily similar to the current task, are not guaranteed to be relevant, and are not instructions to follow verbatim. Variable placeholders like <RECORD_NAME> or <VALUE> stand for instance-specific values; replace them with values from the current task. ## Workflow memory <SKILL_LIBRARY> ## Reference trajectories --- Reference trajectory 1 --- Actions (<N> steps): 1. <ACTION_1> ... --- Reference trajectory 2 --- ... End of help. Now act on the current task; do not mention this help in your output.
⬇ Below is a web-navigation skill learned entirely from offline Mind2Web training trajectories. Apply only the relevant workflows and rules; adapt labels and values to the current page. <SKILL_LIBRARY> End of learned skill. Now choose the next action for the current task. Subgoal coverage: Reference 1 supports: <SUBGOAL>; <SUBGOAL> ... Below are task-matched reference trajectories selected because they cover different reusable subgoals of the current task. Their goals are withheld. Compose only the relevant parts; do not treat any complete trajectory as a recipe for the live site. --- Reference trajectory 1 --- Actions (<N> steps): 1. <ACTION_1> ... End of task-matched workflow references. Below are additional exploration trajectories sampled at RANDOM. They are not claimed to match the current task. Use them only as generic examples of available UI actions when the task-matched patterns are incomplete. --- Reference trajectory 1 --- ... End of random exploration references. Use the reference only as hints; the live site may differ. ## Your task <TASK_GOAL>

A.6 Retrieval Prompts

Workflow-based retrieval (Appendix B) uses two prompts, both at temperature 0. Offline, the annotation prompt labels each training trajectory with the workflows it instantiates, seeing only the trajectory’s actions. For each test task, the planner prompt decomposes the task goal into subgoals and maps each to workflows. The workflow inventory holds the library’s workflows, except that the WorkArena planner receives the whole library, including its skills.

⬇ You label which reusable WORKFLOWS a web-navigation solution uses. You are given an inventory of named workflows (each a "Workflow: <name>" header with numbered steps) and ONE item to label -- either an action trace or a task goal. Return the subset of workflow NAMES that the item instantiates / would require. Rules: - Output ONLY workflow names from the inventory, one per line, verbatim (the snake_case name after "Workflow:"). No numbering, prose, or code fences. - If no inventory workflow applies, output the single sentinel NONE. Never return an empty response. - Include a workflow only if the item clearly uses (trace) or requires (goal) it. Omit ones that do not apply. It is fine to return several names. - Do not invent names that are absent from the inventory.
⬇ Decompose one web-navigation goal into the ordered reusable workflows needed to complete it. Return ONLY a JSON object with this shape: {"subgoals":[{"text":"short action-oriented subgoal","workflows":["name"]}]} Rules: - Preserve execution order and every explicit constraint (search, dates, filters, sorting, selection, cart/checkout, and so on). - Use only workflow names from the supplied inventory, verbatim. - A subgoal may have several workflows or an empty list when the inventory has no adequate workflow. Never invent a workflow name. - Prefer 1-6 concise subgoals. Do not include concrete solutions or UI labels. - Do not wrap the JSON in markdown.

Appendix B Workflow-Based Retrieval Details

Recall that in Section 2.3, we select demonstrations that together cover the subgoals of a new task, using the optimized workflows 𝒲∗\mathcal{W}^{*} as an intermediate representation. We describe the full procedure here in four steps: (1) annotating training trajectories with workflows offline, (2) planning subgoals for a new task, (3) scoring each trajectory against each subgoal, and (4) greedily selecting trajectories that cover the subgoals.

Workflow Annotation. Offline, we annotate each training trajectory τ\tau with the workflows it instantiates:

Z⁡(τ)⊆𝒲∗.Z(\tau)\subseteq\mathcal{W}^{*}. (3)

For example, a trajectory that searches for an item, applies a filter, and submits a form may be annotated with three corresponding workflows. Each workflow w∈𝒲∗w\in\mathcal{W}^{*} then carries a weight that decreases with the number of training trajectories that instantiate it. A workflow shared by most of the training trajectories therefore contributes little to a match, while a rare one contributes most. The weight enters the workflow component of the relevance score below.

Subgoal Planning. For a new task, a planner decomposes the task goal into an ordered collection of subgoals:

P⁡(g)=[(u1,W1),…,(um,Wm)],P(g)=\left[(u_{1},W_{1}),\ldots,(u_{m},W_{m})\right], (4)

where uju_{j} is a subgoal and Wj⊆𝒲∗W_{j}\subseteq\mathcal{W}^{*} contains workflows that may accomplish it. We therefore compare training trajectories and task goals in a shared procedural space.

Relevance Scoring. We assign each trajectory and subgoal pair a relevance score

R⁡(τ,u)=Combine⁡(Rworkflow,Rsemantic,Rsite).R(\tau,u)=\operatorname{Combine}\left(R_{\mathrm{workflow}},R_{\mathrm{semantic}},R_{\mathrm{site}}\right). (5)

The workflow component measures weighted overlap between Z⁡(τ)Z(\tau) and the workflows associated with uu. The semantic component separates trajectories that instantiate the same broad workflow for different purposes. The site component adds a small preference for demonstrations from a compatible website. We treat only sufficiently confident matches as task-relevant.

Greedy Selection. Let UU be the set of subgoals that remain uncovered. The selector repeatedly chooses the trajectory that best covers the current set:

τ∗=arg​maxτ​Coverage​(τ,U).\tau^{*}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\tau}\operatorname{Coverage}(\tau,U). (6)

After selecting τ∗\tau^{*}, we remove the subgoals it supports from UU. We stop when the task is covered, no confident match remains, or the demonstration budget (k=8k{=}8, Section 3) is reached.

The matched set ℰmatched​(g)\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{matched}}(g) contains demonstrations supported by workflow evidence. The exploration set ℰexplore​(g)\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{explore}}(g) contains a small number of deterministically sampled examples, and retrieval slots not filled by confident matches are assigned to exploration. If no workflow can be associated with the task, then ℰmatched​(g)=∅\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{matched}}(g)=\varnothing and we fall back entirely to deterministic random retrieval. On Mind2Web, the prompt labels each matched example with the subgoals it supports and presents exploratory examples separately as generic demonstrations. On WorkArena, all kk demonstrations appear in one list without subgoal labels (Section A.5).

Appendix C Hyperparameters

Table 5 lists the settings of skill optimization, workflow-based retrieval, and the test-time agent. All runs use inferred goals and the two-stage schedule of Section 2.2, and they validate on the full dev split without a curriculum. Unless noted, the settings are shared across WorkArena L1, WorkArena L2, and Mind2Web and across backbones. The Mistral-3.5 deployment samples every call, including the predictor and the agent, at temperature 0.7 and top-pp 0.95.

Appendix D Data Processing and Statistics

Recall that we learn from successful oracle trajectories on WorkArena and from annotator-recorded trajectories on Mind2Web (Section 3). Table 6 lists the resulting counts. Section 3 describes which WorkArena task families we remove. On both WorkArena levels, the test instances are other seeds of the same task templates as the training instances. We split the WorkArena training trajectories into train and dev by trajectory hash, which gives a roughly even split. The Mind2Web training trajectories need more processing, which we describe below.

Mind2Web. Online-Mind2Web provides 300 live tasks, each with a start URL and a difficulty label, but no demonstrations. We therefore draw training trajectories from the original Mind2Web training set, which holds 1,009 trajectories. Online-Mind2Web also does not publish the Mind2Web domain and subdomain labels. We label each online task with one Mind2Web category (e.g., Travel →\rightarrow Airlines or Shopping →\rightarrow Auto) using GPT-5.4 on its instruction and website, and allow a none label when no category fits (13 tasks). We keep a test task only when its category also occurs in the original Mind2Web training set. That set has no Info or Service tasks, so this filter removes all online tasks in those two domains and leaves 122 test tasks (29 easy, 54 medium, and 39 hard) across 17 categories. Applying the same filter in the other direction keeps 966 of the 1,009 training trajectories (7,347 of 7,775 actions), since only Travel →\rightarrow Car rental has no matching test task.

We then downsample the 966 trajectories to 640 with a fixed seed so that the category distribution of the training trajectories follows that of the test tasks. An exact match would require duplicate trajectories, because Shopping →\rightarrow Digital covers 18.9%18.9\% of the test tasks but has only 28 training trajectories. We instead cap each category at the trajectories it has and spread the remaining share proportionally over the other categories, so no trajectory appears twice. This lowers the total-variation distance between the training and test category distributions from 0.2990.299 to 0.2040.204. The resulting training set has 640 trajectories, 4,677 actions, and 70 websites, which we split 1:1 into train and dev by trajectory hash (Table 6).

We report two sets of results that support Section 4: the success rates behind the noise sweep, and token and step counts per episode.

Noise Sweep. Recall that in Section 4.2, we rebuild every method from perturbed WorkArena training pools with increasing interruption rates qq. Table 7 lists the success rates plotted in Figure 4.

Token and Step Counts. Recall that in Section 4.2, we attribute TeleTune’s extra input tokens to a longer per-step prompt, since its episode lengths stay within the baseline range. Table 8 gives the average input and output tokens per episode, and Table 9 gives the average number of steps.
